performers: Titta Ruffo, baritone; Josef Pasternack, conductor
intro: “Largo al factotum” is Figaro’s entrance aria in Act I of Il barbiere di Siviglia, sung as he arrives at dawn with a guitar round his neck. Titta Ruffo recorded it acoustically for Victor in 1920.

cues.title: Figaro’s self-portrait, Allegro vivace
cues.text: The Allegro vivace in 6/8 carries Figaro’s self-portrait. He describes himself as always ready, always in demand and delighted with his trade, and repeats his own name many times.
cues.evidence: Ricordi full score, reprinted by Dover, pp. 54–61: Allegro vivace in 6/8, with Figaro’s repeated name and self-congratulations. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/c/c8/IMSLP517981-PMLP7237-Rossini_-_Il_barbiere_di_Siviglia_-_Act_I_(orch._score)_(etc).pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Figaro’s tools and trade
cues.text: Sterbini gave Figaro razors, combs, lancets and scissors. Besides shaving, this barber lets blood and carries messages between lovers.
cues.evidence: Sterbini, Act I, scene 2: the inventory begins “Rasori e pettini”; the later recitative names Figaro’s services to the unmarried and widowed. In the Ricordi full score, p. 66, the customers’ calls include “presto il biglietto” (quick, the note). https://www.librettidopera.it/barb_siv/rid.html https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/c/c8/IMSLP517981-PMLP7237-Rossini_-_Il_barbiere_di_Siviglia_-_Act_I_(orch._score)_(etc).pdf

cues.title: Customers’ requests and “Figaro” calls
cues.text: At “Tutti mi chiedono” Figaro acts out his customers’ demands for a wig, a shave and a bloodletting. After the repeated calls of his name he pleads for one person at a time. At “Pronto prontissimo” he boasts that he is as quick as lightning.
cues.evidence: Ricordi full score, reprinted by Dover, pp. 65–70: “Tutti mi chiedono”, the customers’ requests and repeated “Figaro” calls, followed by “Pronto prontissimo”. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/c/c8/IMSLP517981-PMLP7237-Rossini_-_Il_barbiere_di_Siviglia_-_Act_I_(orch._score)_(etc).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Titta Ruffo (baritone — Figaro), Josef Pasternack (conductor), Unidentified orchestra (orchestral accompaniment)
fields.note: Bolig and Milmo identify Pasternack as conductor. The label states ‘Baritone with orchestra’; neither it nor the consulted discography names the orchestral players.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Figaro’s Italian-language entrance aria, recorded as a standalone acoustic disc side
fields.note: The label identifies Act I, a baritone and orchestral accompaniment. This is the published aria side, not a complete opera or a recording of the surrounding recitatives. The performing edition, cuts and exact studio orchestration are not established. The listening guide groups broad passages from the historical full score; it does not claim word-level synchronisation.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: All three sources associate matrix C-23945, take 2, with this date. It is not Ruffo’s separate 1912 recording of the same aria.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Bolig and Milmo list Camden for this matrix. No particular studio room or street address is established.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The accompanying National Jukebox label image shows a red Victrola label and the Victor Talking Machine Company name.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The transferred carrier’s label reads 6263-A. The discographies connect the same matrix with both Victor numbers and HMV DB 405; the exact pressing date of the photographed copy is unknown.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: C-23945, take 2; side A of Victor 6263
fields.note: The matrix and take are identified by the catalogue metadata and discography; the label establishes the side. Stamper and pressing-run details are not established.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Library of Congress Packard Campus for Audio Visual Conservation; National Jukebox MP3 mirrored by Hessel Digital Library
fields.note: These are the digitisation and mirror credits stated in the Internet Archive item, which links to the original National Jukebox record. The Library of Congress record identifies its source disc as Victor 6263-A, matrix C-23945-2. No individual transfer engineer is identified.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Library of Congress digitisation date is not supplied. The mirror describes a 30 September 2026 retrieval of the LOC MP3; that is a copying event, not the recording or digitisation date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: The mirror reports a bit-exact copy of the Library of Congress MP3, with no processing added by the uploader.
fields.note: The uploader states a bit-exact copy. The Library of Congress master WAV of Victor 6263-A has the same duration, 247.78 seconds, and the same performance at the same speed and pitch throughout; byte identity with the Library’s own access MP3 has not been checked. The original stylus, playback speed, equalisation, noise reduction and restoration settings remain unknown.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Rossini’s music and Sterbini’s Italian libretto are out of copyright under ordinary life-plus-70 terms.
fields.note: Rossini died in 1868 and Sterbini in 1831. This assessment covers the historical work, not unidentified modern arrangements or editions.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: first published no later than 1924, on double-faced Victor 6263; the mirror carries the Public Domain Mark.
fields.note: Selected under the project’s us-published-before-cutoff rule. Victor’s 1924 catalogue lists the Ruffo Largo al factotum on 6263, which is absent from the 1923 catalogue; the Library of Congress identifies 6263-A as this matrix. The same recording was also issued on single-faced Victor 88391, replacing Ruffo’s 1912 recording under that number; the mirror states first publication in 1920, but no dated release source was found. On either date, US protection ended no later than 31 December 2024. The Public Domain Mark is a status declaration, not a new licence grant or a worldwide clearance.

composer.background:
On 20 February 1816, at Rome’s Teatro Argentina, a barber came on stage announcing that everyone needed him. Figaro could shave a chin, deliver a letter and arrange a marriage, and he called out his own name so many times that the part tested even his singer. The opera was advertised as Almaviva, ossia L’inutile precauzione. Its first night failed. Within a few performances the public had changed its mind about Rossini’s Barber of Seville.

Gioachino Rossini was born in Pesaro on 29 February 1792. His father Giuseppe played horn and trumpet; his mother Anna Guidarini became a professional singer. The boy travelled with them as they worked. In Lugo, from 1802, the priest Giuseppe Malerbi taught him composition and introduced him to Haydn and Mozart. At Bologna’s Liceo Musicale, which he entered in 1806, Rossini studied cello, piano and counterpoint. Before he composed operas he worked in the theatre as a musician, singer and keyboard player.
